summary.text: Couple the evolutions for masses \(n\) and \(n+1\) by viewing the extra unit as a token that stays put or moves one site right according to the parity of the local mass; comparison with the leading block of ones shows that at the hitting time for \(n\), its position \(p\) satisfies \(n-p\in\{1,2\}\). Once the mass-\(n\) configuration is stable, the token moves right through the ones to site \(n\), giving the exact recurrence \(A(n+1)=A(n)+(n-p)\).

full_proof.text:
Let configurations be indexed by the nonnegative integers, with position 0 the leftmost cell. It is convenient first to regard a finite configuration as an infinite sequence with zeros appended. Thus a configuration is a function
\[
f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N
\]
of finite support. One evolution step is the operator \(T\) defined by
\[
(Tf)(i)=\left\lceil\frac{f(i)}2\right\rceil+
\begin{cases}
0,&i=0,\\[2mm]
\left\lfloor\dfrac{f(i-1)}2\right\rfloor,&i>0.
\end{cases}
\]
Equivalently, using integer division,
\[
(Tf)(i)=\frac{f(i)+1}{2}+
\begin{cases}0,&i=0,\\ f(i-1)/2,&i>0.\end{cases}
\]
This is exactly the cellular-automaton rule: a cell retains the ceiling of half its mass, and sends the floor of half its mass one place to the right.

For \(n\geq 1\), let
\[
I_n(i)=\begin{cases}n,&i=0,\\0,&i>0,\end{cases}
\qquad
U_n(i)=\begin{cases}1,&i<n,\\0,&i\geq n.\end{cases}
\]
The trajectory of initial mass \(n\) is
\[
F_{n,t}=T^t I_n.
\]
The target stable state is \(U_n\). We shall first prove that this target is reached and define
\[
A(n)=\min\{t:F_{n,t}=U_n\}.
\]
Later we verify that this infinite-sequence formulation has exactly the same hitting time as the finite-list definition of \(a(n)\) in the question.

## 1. Basic properties and existence of the hitting time

Call \(f\) gapless if a zero is always followed by a zero:
\[
f(i)=0\implies f(i+1)=0.
\]
Thus the nonzero entries of a gapless finite-support configuration occupy an initial interval. The initial state \(I_n\) is gapless. Moreover, \(T\) preserves gaplessness. Indeed, if \((Tf)(i)=0\), both nonnegative summands in its definition vanish. In particular \(f(i)=0\). Gaplessness gives \(f(i+1)=0\), and then
\[
(Tf)(i+1)=\left\lceil\frac{f(i+1)}2\right\rceil+
\left\lfloor\frac{f(i)}2\right\rfloor=0.
\]
Therefore every \(F_{n,t}\) is gapless.

If \(f(i)=0\) for every \(i\geq M\), then \((Tf)(i)=0\) for every \(i\geq M+1\). Consequently \(F_{n,t}\) is supported in \([0,t+1)\).

Mass is conserved. If \(f\) is supported in \([0,M)\), then summing \(Tf\) over \([0,M+1)\) gives
\[
\sum_{i=0}^{M}(Tf)(i)
 =\sum_{i=0}^{M-1}\left(\left\lceil\frac{f(i)}2\right\rceil+
 \left\lfloor\frac{f(i)}2\right\rfloor\right)
 =\sum_{i=0}^{M-1}f(i),
\]
because the retained part of the mass remains at \(i\), while the sent part appears at \(i+1\). Hence every \(F_{n,t}\) has total mass \(n\).

Gaplessness and mass conservation give a stronger, time-independent support bound: every \(F_{n,t}\) is supported in \([0,n)\). To see this, if a gapless configuration of total mass \(n\) had a nonzero entry at some \(i\geq n\), then all entries at positions \(0,1,\dots,i\) would be nonzero, so its total mass would be at least \(i+1>n\), a contradiction.

We next show that the process must stabilize. For a configuration supported in \([0,n)\), define its first moment and its one-step work by
\[
M(f)=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}i f(i),
\qquad
W(f)=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\left\lfloor\frac{f(i)}2\right\rfloor.
\]
Every unit of mass sent to the right increases the first moment by one, while retained mass does not move. Therefore
\[
M(Tf)=M(f)+W(f).
\]
This also follows directly by shifting the index in the sum of received masses.

A configuration on \([0,n)\), of mass \(n\), all of whose entries are at most 1 must equal \(U_n\): there are \(n\) available positions and total mass \(n\), so every one of those positions must contain exactly 1. It follows that if \(F_{n,t}\ne U_n\), then some entry is at least 2, and hence
\[
W(F_{n,t})\geq 1.
\]
On the other hand, because all mass lies at positions at most \(n-1\),
\[
M(F_{n,t})\leq (n-1)n.
\]
Initially the moment is zero. If the target had not been reached in the first \((n-1)n+1\) steps, the moment would increase by at least one at each of those steps and would therefore exceed \((n-1)n\), contradicting the preceding bound. Thus \(U_n\) is reached and \(A(n)\) is well-defined.

The target is fixed by the evolution: \(T U_n=U_n\). Indeed, at position 0 its value remains \(\lceil 1/2\rceil=1\); for \(0<i<n\), it is \(\lceil1/2\rceil+\lfloor1/2\rfloor=1\); and at and beyond \(n\) both contributing terms are zero. In particular, once the target is reached it persists forever.

## 2. Coupling masses \(n\) and \(n+1\)

For a configuration \(f\) and a position \(p\), write
\[
f+e_p
\]
for the configuration obtained by adding one unit at position \(p\). There is a fundamental one-step coupling identity:
\[
T(f+e_p)=Tf+e_{p+f(p)\bmod 2}.
\tag{1}
\]
To verify it, only positions \(p\) and \(p+1\) can be affected by the added unit. If \(f(p)\) is even, increasing it by one increases its retained ceiling half by one and leaves its sent floor half unchanged, so the extra unit remains at \(p\). If \(f(p)\) is odd, increasing it by one leaves its retained ceiling half unchanged and increases its sent floor half by one, so the extra unit moves to \(p+1\). This is precisely (1).

Define the position \(P_{n,t}\) of this extra token recursively by
\[
P_{n,0}=0,
\qquad
P_{n,t+1}=P_{n,t}+F_{n,t}(P_{n,t})\bmod 2.
\tag{2}
\]
Since \(I_{n+1}=I_n+e_0\), induction using (1) gives the exact coupling
\[
F_{n+1,t}=F_{n,t}+e_{P_{n,t}}
\tag{3}
\]
for every \(t\). Thus the extra unit either stays put or moves one step right at each time, and it moves exactly when the mass under it in the \(n\)-trajectory is odd.

We need to locate this token when the \(n\)-trajectory first reaches its target. The main device is the length of the leading block of ones. For a finite-support configuration \(f\), define
\[
g(f)=\min\{i:f(i)\ne1\}.
\]
Thus
\[
f(0)=f(1)=\cdots=f(g(f)-1)=1,
\]
and \(f(g(f))\ne1\). For our trajectories this minimum always exists, since \(F_{n,t}(n)=0\). Notice also that
\[
g(U_n)=n.
\]

We first record two facts about the motion of this front.

### Front growth is at most two

For every gapless finite-support \(f\),
\[
g(Tf)\leq g(f)+2.
\tag{4}
\]
Put \(g=g(f)\). Since \(f(g)\ne1\), consider the following exhaustive cases.

* If \(f(g)=0\), gaplessness gives \(f(g+1)=0\). Hence \((Tf)(g+1)=0\), so \(g(Tf)\leq g+1\).
* Suppose \(f(g)=2\). If \(f(g+1)=0\), gaplessness also gives \(f(g+2)=0\), and therefore \((Tf)(g+2)=0\), giving \(g(Tf)\leq g+2\). If instead \(f(g+1)>0\), then at position \(g+1\) the incoming contribution from position \(g\) is \(\lfloor2/2\rfloor=1\), while the retained contribution from \(g+1\) is at least 1. Thus \((Tf)(g+1)\geq2\), so \(g(Tf)\leq g+1\).
* If \(f(g)\geq3\), then \(\lceil f(g)/2\rceil\geq2\), so \((Tf)(g)\geq2\), and \(g(Tf)\leq g\).

This proves (4).

There is a useful strengthening. If the front advances by two, in the sense that
\[
g(Tf)\geq g(f)+2,
\tag{5}
\]
then every entry of \(Tf\) is at most 1. Indeed, write again \(g=g(f)\). Condition (5) says that \((Tf)(g)=(Tf)(g+1)=1\). The incoming contribution at \(g\) from \(g-1\), when \(g>0\), is \(\lfloor1/2\rfloor=0\), and it is also zero when \(g=0\). Since \(f(g)\ne1\), the equation \((Tf)(g)=1\) forces \(f(g)=2\). Then
\[
1=(Tf)(g+1)=\left\lceil\frac{f(g+1)}2\right\rceil+
\left\lfloor\frac22\right\rfloor

gives \(f(g+1)=0\). By gaplessness, all later entries vanish. Hence \(f\) has the special form
\[
(\underbrace{1,\ldots,1}_{g\text{ entries}},2,0,0,\ldots).
\]
A direct application of the update rule shows that every entry of its successor is 0 or 1. Thus (5) indeed implies that \(Tf\) has all entries at most 1.

For the mass-\(n\) trajectory, a successor that is not the target cannot have all entries at most 1, because it has support in \([0,n)\) and total mass \(n\). Therefore, whenever \(F_{n,t+1}\ne U_n\), the strengthening above implies
\[
g(F_{n,t+1})\leq g(F_{n,t})+1.
\tag{6}
\]

### The token remains close to the front

As long as the \(n\)-trajectory has not reached its target,
\[
g(F_{n,t})\leq P_{n,t}+1.
\tag{7}
\]
We prove this by induction on \(t\). At time 0, \(P_{n,0}=0\), and the first non-one entry of \(I_n\) occurs no later than position 1, so (7) holds.

Suppose it holds at time \(t\), and suppose \(F_{n,t+1}\ne U_n\). Then \(F_{n,t}\ne U_n\), because \(U_n\) is fixed. Let
\[
g=g(F_{n,t}),\qquad q=P_{n,t}.
\]
By (6), the new front is at most \(g+1\). If \(q<g\), then the token lies in the leading block of ones, so \(F_{n,t}(q)=1\), and (2) says that it moves to \(q+1\). The induction hypothesis gives \(g\leq q+1\), hence the new front is at most \(q+2=P_{n,t+1}+1\). If \(q\geq g\), then the token does not move left, so \(P_{n,t+1}\geq q\geq g\), and again the new front, which is at most \(g+1\), is at most \(P_{n,t+1}+1\). This proves (7).

## 3. The token position at time \(A(n)\)

Set
\[
p=P_{n,A(n)}.
\]
We prove the two bounds
\[
n-2\leq p\leq n-1.
\tag{8}
\]
They are written this way informally; for \(n=1\) the lower bound simply means \(n\leq p+2\). More precisely, we prove
\[
p\leq n-1,
\qquad
n\leq p+2.
\tag{9}
\]

First we establish the upper bound. We need two observations.

For any time \(t\), the mass at the last possible position satisfies
\[
F_{n,t}(n-1)\leq1.
\tag{10}
\]
Indeed, the support bound says both \(F_{n,t}(n)=0\) and \(F_{n,t+1}(n)=0\). Applying the update rule at position \(n\), the latter equality reads
\[
0=\left\lceil\frac{F_{n,t}(n)}2\right\rceil+
\left\lfloor\frac{F_{n,t}(n-1)}2\right\rfloor
=
\left\lfloor\frac{F_{n,t}(n-1)}2\right\rfloor,
\]
which gives (10).

Furthermore, if \(F_{n,t}(n-1)=1\), then gaplessness implies that every earlier position is nonzero. Since the total mass is \(n\) and there are exactly \(n\) possible positions, all these entries must equal 1. Thus
\[
F_{n,t}(n-1)=1\implies F_{n,t}=U_n.
\tag{11}
\]

We also need that before stabilization the token is strictly left of \(n\):
\[
F_{n,t}\ne U_n\implies P_{n,t}<n.
\tag{12}
\]
Let \(q=P_{n,t}\). By (3), \(F_{n+1,t}=F_{n,t}+e_q\), and the left side is gapless. If \(q>n\), then its value at position \(n\) is zero, because \(F_{n,t}\) is supported below \(n\), whereas its value at the later position \(q\) is positive because of the extra token. This contradicts gaplessness. Hence \(q\leq n\). If \(q=n\), the value at position \(n\) of \(F_{n+1,t}\) is positive. Gaplessness then makes every position below \(n\) positive. At positions below \(n\), the added token changes nothing, so every \(F_{n,t}(i)\), \(i<n\), is positive. Total mass \(n\) then forces \(F_{n,t}=U_n\), contrary to the hypothesis. Thus (12) holds.

If \(A(n)=0\), then \(p=P_{n,0}=0\), and \(p\leq n-1\) follows from \(n\geq1\). Otherwise write \(A(n)=m+1\). At time \(m\) the \(n\)-trajectory is not yet the target, so by (12), \(P_{n,m}<n\). If \(P_{n,m}<n-1\), then the token can move by at most one in the next step, giving \(p\leq n-1\). The only remaining possibility is \(P_{n,m}=n-1\). By (10), the mass under the token is 0 or 1; it cannot be 1, since (11) would say the trajectory had already reached the target. Hence it is 0, so the token does not move. Again \(p=n-1\). This proves the upper bound in (9).

For the lower bound, if \(A(n)=0\), then \(I_n=U_n\). Comparing their values at position 0 gives \(n=1\), and with \(p=0\) we have \(n\leq p+2\).

Now suppose \(A(n)=m+1\). Put
\[
g=g(F_{n,m}),\qquad q=P_{n,m}.
\]
The state at time \(m+1\) is \(U_n\), whose leading-one count is \(n\). By the general two-step front bound (4),
\[
n=g(U_n)=g(TF_{n,m})\leq g+2.
\tag{13}
\]
We claim \(g\leq p\). If \(q\geq g\), this is immediate because the token never moves left, so \(p\geq q\geq g\). If \(q<g\), the token is on a leading 1 and therefore moves from \(q\) to \(q+1\), so \(p=q+1\). Since time \(m\) is preterminal, (7) gives \(g\leq q+1=p\). Combining this with (13) yields \(n\leq p+2\), proving the lower bound in (9).

## 4. Exact recurrence for the hitting times

At time \(A(n)\), the coupling (3) and the definition of \(A(n)\) give
\[
F_{n+1,A(n)}=U_n+e_p,
\qquad p=P_{n,A(n)}.
\tag{14}
\]
By (9), \(p\leq n-1<n\).

When an extra token is placed at a position \(r<n\) of \(U_n\), the mass under it in the base configuration is 1, so one update moves that token exactly one place right while leaving \(U_n\) fixed:
\[
T(U_n+e_r)=U_n+e_{r+1}\qquad(r<n).
\tag{15}
\]
This is also an immediate instance of the coupling identity (1). Iterating (15), for every \(s\) with \(p+s\leq n\),
\[
T^s(U_n+e_p)=U_n+e_{p+s}.
\tag{16}
\]
At \(s=n-p\), the right side is
\[
U_n+e_n=U_{n+1}.
\]
Thus
\[
A(n+1)\leq A(n)+n-p.
\tag{17}
\]

We show that equality holds. First, the \((n+1)\)-trajectory cannot reach \(U_{n+1}\) before time \(A(n)\). Indeed, suppose at some time \(s\) that
\[
F_{n+1,s}=U_{n+1}.
\]
By coupling, this says
\[
F_{n,s}+e_q=U_{n+1},
\qquad q=P_{n,s}.
\tag{18}
\]
At position \(q\), equation (18) implies \(F_{n,s}(q)+1=U_{n+1}(q)\), so necessarily \(q\leq n\). If \(q<n\), then the right side at \(q\) is 1, so \(F_{n,s}(q)=0\). Gaplessness gives \(F_{n,s}(q+1)=0\). But \(q+1\leq n\), the added token is not at \(q+1\), and \(U_{n+1}(q+1)=1\), contradicting (18). Therefore \(q=n\). Comparing (18) at all positions now gives \(F_{n,s}=U_n\). Hence \(s\geq A(n)\).

It remains to exclude times strictly between \(A(n)\) and \(A(n)+n-p\). Such a time is \(A(n)+s\) with \(0\leq s<n-p\). By (14) and (16), its configuration is
\[
U_n+e_{p+s}.
\]
Since \(p+s<n\), this configuration has value 2 at position \(p+s\), whereas \(U_{n+1}\) has value 1 there. Thus it is not yet the target. Consequently
\[
A(n+1)=A(n)+n-p.
\tag{19}
\]

The bounds (9) say
\[
p\leq n-1\quad\text{and}\quad p\geq n-2,
\]
with the second inequality understood through \(n\leq p+2\). Since \(p\) and \(n\) are integers, this means
\[
n-p\in\{1,2\}.
\]
Equation (19) therefore yields
\[
A(n+1)=A(n)+1
\quad\text{or}\quad
A(n+1)=A(n)+2.
\tag{20}
\]

## 5. Agreement with the original finite-list automaton

It remains to connect \(A(n)\) with the sequence \(a(n)\), whose configurations are finite lists and whose update discards trailing zeros.

For a finite list \(L\), let \(\widehat L(i)\) be its \(i\)-th entry when \(i\) is within the list and 0 otherwise. Before trimming, the list update forms two lists of equal length:

* the retained masses \(\lceil L_j/2\rceil\), followed by one zero;
* an initial zero, followed by the sent masses \(\lfloor L_j/2\rfloor\).

It then adds these lists coordinatewise. Therefore the zero extension of this untrimmed update is exactly \(T\widehat L\). Removing trailing zeros does not alter the zero extension. Hence, if \(C\) denotes the finite-list cellular-automaton step,
\[
\widehat{C(L)}=T\widehat L.
\tag{21}
\]
By induction,
\[
\widehat{C^t([n])}=T^t\widehat{[n]}=T^tI_n=F_{n,t}.
\tag{22}
\]
The fold over a range of length \(t\) used in the definition of \(a(n)\) is simply another notation for applying \(C\) exactly \(t\) times.

The zero extension of the list containing \(n\) copies of 1 is exactly \(U_n\). Also, both \(C^t([n])\) and the list of \(n\) ones have no trailing zeros: the update explicitly trims all trailing zeros, the initial list \([n]\) has nonzero last entry because \(n\geq1\), and a list of ones plainly has no trailing zero. Two finite lists with no trailing zeros and identical zero extensions are equal. Indeed, their last nonzero positions determine the same length, and then equality of the zero extensions gives equality at every list position.

It follows from (22) that, for every \(t\),
\[
C^t([n])=[1,1,\ldots,1]\ \text{(\(n\) entries)}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
F_{n,t}=U_n.
\]
Thus the sets of stable times in the finite-list and infinite-sequence descriptions coincide, and so do their least elements:
\[
a(n)=A(n)\qquad(n\geq1).
\tag{23}
\]
Finally, substituting (23) into (20) proves that for every integer \(n\geq1\),
\[
\boxed{\ a(n+1)=a(n)+1\quad\text{or}\quad a(n+1)=a(n)+2\ }.
\]
Equivalently, every finite difference \(a(n+1)-a(n)\) is either \(1\) or \(2\), as required.
